title: Prose and Table 2 disagree on the seed-1 patch difference at 1e-5, and the reconciliation note is ambiguous
quote: A is −0.7 [−3.3, +2.0] points of pass@1 at seed 0 and +0.0 [−2.7, +2.7] at
explanation: Table 2 gives pass@1 changes at 1e-5 of A,0 = −2.7, B,0 = −3.3, A,1 = −3.3, B,1 = −4.0. The B-minus-A differences are therefore −0.6 (seed 0, i.e. −0.67 = one problem) and −0.7 (seed 1). The text reports −0.7 at seed 0 and +0.0 at seed 1 'recomputed from the saved generations'. The parenthetical says Table 2 'lists values from the run logs that differ by one problem, giving −0.7', without saying which seed this applies to. Reading the table, it is seed 1 (−0.7 versus recomputed +0.0), not seed 0 (−0.6, which matches −0.7 up to rounding). The headline table in the paper therefore carries a number the authors themselves say is wrong, in the very comparison used to conclude the patch has no effect. The Table 2 caption reports only a pass@8 discrepancy (58.0 vs 58.7) for B, seed 1 and does not mention that the pass@1 value for this run is also affected. The direction of the conclusion is unchanged (both are about zero), but the paper should either correct Table 2 or state per seed and metric which values were replaced. It would also help to keep one scoring source for all numbers; at present Table 1, Table 2 and the prose mix log-based and re-scored values.
source_section: 4.3 The Patch Control Could Not Detect an Effect

title: Design P explanations: the selection==eval confound cannot produce a decline, and the 4.5x-dose explanation is hard to square with the 5e-4 runs
quote: both datasets’ pools; it scores on the problems it selects from; and it trains on
explanation: Section 4.1 lists three confounds (shared adapter over two datasets, scoring on the problems it selects from, about 4.5x more training examples) and concludes the design 'cannot be read causally' and that 'no run separates these explanations'. I checked this against the paper's own numbers. (i) Selection==eval can only bias accuracy upward: training on the model's own verified-correct solutions to the very problems it is scored on should inflate, not deflate, exam accuracy. It therefore cannot be an explanation of a fall from 50.0% to 18.6% pass@1; it makes the collapse more surprising, not less interpretable. (ii) The dose explanation is quantitatively doubtful. Each round's model is a single adapter trained on the previous pool, with optimizer steps equal to half the pool (Section 3.4). Design P at 1e-5 with 3,962 examples is about 1,980 steps x 1e-5, roughly 0.02 in step-times-rate units at most (before linear decay). Design I at 5e-4 with about 390-440 examples is about 200 steps x 5e-4, roughly 0.1, about five times larger, yet it loses only 4-11 pass@1 points (Table 2), and no-filter at 3.6x the steps (about 700 steps) loses a similar amount (Table 3). Step-times-rate is a crude proxy, but nothing in the paper's own evidence shows a dose-response steep enough for a 4.5x pool at 1e-5 to cause a 31-point collapse. This leaves the dataset mixing (one adapter on GSM8K plus MATH data, with a much larger and easier GSM8K share of accepted examples) as the least-tested candidate. Section 4.4's own statement that no-filter at 3-4x the steps does not decline more than Run A cuts against the dose reading, while the same section uses dose to dismiss the no-filter comparison. The paper should state which of the three explanations the existing data disfavour instead of treating them as equally open, and note that the intro's 'does not reproduce under isolation' is itself a causal-sounding framing the section says it cannot support.

title: The 'replicate' reading of same-seed A/B and the +5.3 to −7.3 'flip' rest on single-sample pass@1; sample accuracy shows a much smaller flip
quote: is +5.3 at seed 1 and −7.3 [−14.0, −0.7] at seed 2, a sign ﬂip from pools that
explanation: The paper uses the B-minus-A sign flip in round-2 pass@1 (+5.3, −7.3) as the central evidence of large training-trajectory noise (Section 3.4, 4.4), and so for treating same-seed A/B as 'closer to two replicates than four' and for calling reported intervals optimistic. I recomputed from Table 2 at 5e-4. B minus A in pass@1: seed 1 = −4.7 − (−10.0) = +5.3; seed 2 = −11.3 − (−4.0) = −7.3 (correct). But pass@1 uses one draw per problem (Section 3.4), so for p around 0.3 and n = 150 the sampling SD of a single pass@1 is about 3.7 points and the SD of a difference of two independent runs about 5.2 points. A 5-7 point gap is therefore only about 1-1.4 SD of pure resampling noise and does not by itself reveal trajectory instability. On the paper's own preferred, lower-variance measure (sample accuracy over four draws), B minus A is −6.7 − (−8.3) = +1.6 at seed 1 and −9.2 − (−4.7) = −4.5 at seed 2: a smaller flip. For pass@4 it is +5.3 and −4.6. Further problems with the replicate reading: (a) the seed-2 B-minus-A interval [−14.0, −0.7] excludes zero, which the text dismisses as 'trajectory noise' without showing that noise (rather than the patch) is the cause, since no true replicate (same seed, same verifier, differently shuffled data) exists; (b) same-seed pairs share exam partition and selection set, whereas Section 3.4's 'one same-configuration replicate pair' (3.2 points apart) is not identified and cannot be matched to any pair in Tables 1-2; the three-seed 1e-4 runs differ by 5 points in round-2 sample accuracy (32.2, 27.2, 27.5) but those also differ in exam partition, so training noise and partition noise are not separated; (c) the one-seed-pair evidence is then used to inflate all detectable-effect numbers ('probably larger') with no estimate of the actual variance. A correct replicate estimate needs at least two runs that differ only in training randomness, or a variance decomposition across seeds for a measure like sample accuracy.

title: 'No detectable gain' is stated as a per-interval null, but the pooled sign pattern points to a decline that the text declines to name
quote: We read this as a possible small decline, not an established
explanation: The paper makes no multiplicity correction and says it rests conclusions on 'patterns across runs and seeds', but does not actually analyse the pattern. From Table 2 (MATH-500 A/B runs, excluding C and controls): sample-accuracy changes are all negative in 9 of 9 runs at 1e-5, 1e-4 and 2e-4 (−2.4, −1.5, −3.2, −1.2, −1.5, −3.7, −1.0, −3.5, −3.8; mean about −2.4), and pass@1 changes are negative in 12 of 13 A/B runs (only A,1 at 1e-4 is +0.7), all 13 at or below +0.7. A one-sided sign test treating runs as independent gives p of about 0.002 (12 of 13) and 0.002 (9 of 9), though runs share the same 150 problems within a seed, so the real evidence is weaker; the correct analysis is a pooled mixed model over seeds and problems, which the paper does not report. The 'no gain' claim itself is safe against multiplicity (no interval is positive, so there is no false-positive to correct), but the descriptive claims that are quoted use post hoc subsets ('only for B at seed 0', 'five of six runs', 'the six include two same-seed pairs') that are exactly where multiplicity matters. The text also hedges the declines ('possible small decline, not an established one') while treating no-gain as established, which is an asymmetric standard. Since the Abstract and Section 5.1 state the null as 'not detectably' better, the paper should either report the pooled estimate and interval (which likely excludes zero for sample accuracy), or explain why a consistent sign pattern is not informative. Also, the observed upper limits (up to +8 for pass@1, +2.2 for sample accuracy) are much tighter than the 10-point 'detectable effect', so the statement 'a gain of the size the design could detect' undersells what the data exclude for sample accuracy and oversells what they exclude for pass@1.

title: Rate dependence is not shown: 1e-5 and 1e-4 give the same decline, which undercuts the 'adapter did little at 1e-5' rationale
quote: length and cap-hit share, barely change, which is weak evidence that the adapter
explanation: Section 4.4 motivates the higher-rate runs by 'Because 10−5 changed the MATH-500 outputs little' and Section 4.2 supports that with unchanged length and cap-hit share. But Table 2 shows the mean sample-accuracy change is about −2.1 at 1e-5 (A/B, four runs: −2.4, −1.5, −3.2, −1.2) and about −2.1 at 1e-4 (−1.5, −3.7, −1.0), i.e. a tenfold increase in rate changes nothing, whereas 5e-4 gives −8.3 and −4.7 and 2e-4 gives −3.5 and −3.8. The decline therefore does not scale with rate over 1e-5 to 1e-4, and at seed 2 it is 'almost flat' (3.7, 3.8, 4.7) over 1e-4 to 5e-4. The only monotone trace is seed 1 (1.5, 3.5, 8.3) from a single partition. The text's 'may grow with the rate' is thus based on one seed, while the other seed shows a flat response, and the 1e-5 runs (which differ in k, rounds and metric) are not on this axis anyway. If the 1e-5 adapter did little, a decline of similar size at 1e-4 is difficult to attribute to the adapter at all; alternatively the 1e-5 adapter did change behaviour (Run C falls 12.7 points at the same rate with about 2x steps), so 'changed the outputs little' is not a safe premise. In either case, causal statements like 'decline may grow with the rate' and, in the Introduction, 'most clearly at the highest rate' need to be restricted to what two seeds at 5e-4 show, and the constant floor of about −2 at low rate (possibly a measurement or round-0 sampling artefact, since round-0 pass@1 itself varies from 29.3 to 33.3 across seeds) should be discussed.

title: Cap-share decomposition is not reproducible from the main text, and a direct computation gives a seed-2 share far above the reported 52-72%
quote: attributes 12–30% of the decline to the cap share in the three original seed-1
explanation: Table 1 gives the ingredients for a simple decomposition: sample accuracy = f x a, with f the finished share (1 minus the cap-hit share) and a the finished accuracy. For A at 5e-4, seed 1: round-0 cap share 43.2% (f0 = 0.568), round-2 46.2% (f2 = 0.538), sample accuracy 33.7 to 25.3. Then a0 = 59.3% and the cap-share term (Δf x a0) = −3.0 x 0.593 = −1.8 points, about 21% of the −8.4 decline, inside the stated 12-30%. For seed 2: cap share 43.0% to 51.2% (Δf = −8.2 points), sample accuracy 30.8 to 26.2, a0 = 54.0%, so the cap-share term is −8.2 x 0.54 = −4.4 points, about 96% of the −4.6 decline, versus the reported 52-72%. The reported matched finished accuracy for A,2 is −5.5 points, which would add a further −3 points for a total near −7.5, larger than the actual −4.7, so the three parts as described cannot be additive without a large positive cross term. The text never says how the 'three-part decomposition' and 'matched' measures treat problem mix, so these figures cannot be checked. The numbers also vary widely by run (12-30%, −2%, 5%, 52-72%), and for seed 2 the cap share, not finished accuracy, carries the majority of the decline, which conflicts with the Introduction and contribution bullet ('What appears, most clearly at the highest rate, is lower accuracy on the solutions the model does finish') and with the statement that finished accuracy 'carries the whole change' at lower rates (those declines are of the same size at seed 2: 3.7 to 3.8). The mechanism is thus seed-dependent, and magnitudes of declines alone (flat across rates at seed 2) hide different mechanisms. Please define the decomposition in the main text and reconcile it with Table 1.

title: Pool-size and 'differ by' figures use inconsistent units and values across sections and tables
quote: \dfrac appears in 0.50–0.73% of generations, so the kept pools diﬀer by 3–4
explanation: The A-versus-B pool difference is given as 0–4 examples in Section 3.2, 3–4 examples in Section 4.3 and 0–3 examples in Section 4.4; these ranges are not nested sensibly (3-4 vs 0-3) and do not say which learning rate and k they apply to. Separately, Table 3 reports kept pools of 440 to 326 and 424 to 350 (examples; up to 4 per problem), while Table 1's added/lost counts are problems solved by at least one of 4 samples (22/33 and 26/36), and Section 3.4 states added minus lost equals 150 x Δpass@k. I checked this identity against Table 1 and it holds for all seven rows (e.g. 22 − 33 = −11 = 150 x (−7.3%)). But a reader comparing 'problems added/lost' of −11 with a pool contraction of 114 examples (440 to 326) may take them to describe the same quantity; the Table 3 caption does not state the unit, and does not state that round 0 to round 2 means the round-2 model uses the middle pool (392 or 386) rather than the endpoint figures in the column. The 'about 195 steps' (392/2 = 196, 386/2 = 193) is consistent, and the 4.5x pool ratio (3,962 vs 872) checks out. The unit and range inconsistencies are minor but affect how a reader judges the 'trajectory noise from near-identical pools' argument, which depends on exactly how identical the pools are.
source_section: 4.3 The Patch Control Could Not Detect an Effect

title: No-filter versus filtered comparison is summarised through pass@4 only; other metrics show a mixed or reversed sign
quote: lower on pass@4 at both seeds (round-2 diﬀerences −2.0 and −5.3
explanation: The text says removing the filter 'is not better than keeping it beyond noise and is lower on pass@4 at both seeds'. From Table 2/3 at 5e-4: pass@4 no-filter minus A = −2.0 (seed 1) and −5.3 (seed 2), correct. But pass@1 no-filter minus A in round 2 is 27.3 − 23.3 = +4.0 at seed 1 and 22.7 − 27.3 = −4.6 at seed 2, and sample accuracy is −8.2 − (−8.3) = +0.1 at seed 1 and −10.2 − (−4.7) = −5.5 at seed 2. So the direction is consistent only for one of the three measures, and at seed 1 the sample accuracy (the paper's preferred measure) is identical for the two arms. Selecting the one metric with a consistent sign, among several available, is the same selection that the paper elsewhere warns about (post hoc metrics). Moreover, the no-filter arm uses 3.6x the optimizer steps (1,400 examples against 392 or 386), yet its decline is no larger than the filtered run at seed 1; that undermines the idea that a larger dose should be expected to produce more decline, which the paper uses in Section 4.1 to explain the Design P collapse. The sentence should report all three measures and conclude plainly that the comparison is uninformative, rather than leaning on the pass@4 sign.
